summary:
San Luis Potosí stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains unevenly implemented. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and set out a per-state compliance picture showing that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

San Luis Potosí is among the states that have acted. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, following a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law that created an administrative recognition procedure with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree, and it is listed among the states that enacted a gender-identity law that year.

Formal recognition does not translate into even treatment. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people is recorded nationally. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, and the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Document delays carry their own exposure. Human Rights Watch's report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police; the report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Official responses remain partial. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, a statute named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished and which activists describe as critical to their sense of safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009. In San Luis Potosí it took effect on 21 May 2019 after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019.
tangentialFactors:
The national direction is toward wider recognition: 22 of 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by March 2025, which places San Luis Potosí's 2019 procedure within the majority pattern rather than an exception. Human Rights Watch nonetheless warns that implementation differs sharply from state to state, so a procedure's existence elsewhere is a poor guide to how it runs in practice.

The distance between statute and enforcement is the recurring national finding. Beer's LSE USAPP analysis reports that progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly and cautions against reading formal rights as evidence of safety from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Where recognition has stalled, consequences are concrete. Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents with documents that contradict their lived identity, which then amplifies discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. Comparable obstruction in San Luis Potosí would produce the same exposure, and visitors should expect document checks to be a point of friction wherever papers do not match presentation.

Violence indicators continue to trend upward. localsOnly:
San Luis Potosí operates an administrative route to legal gender recognition created by the 2019 reform of its Civil Registry Law, with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree; the state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019.

The state's hate-crime statutes recognise motivation by gender and sexual preference, giving residents a basis for aggravated treatment of bias-motivated offences.

Local anti-discrimination law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender but does not name gender identity, leaving gender-identity-based complaints on weaker statutory footing than orientation-based ones.

Same-sex marriage took effect in San Luis Potosí on 21 May 2019 after the state Congress approved it 14-12 on 16 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the state from the same month. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not show whether San Luis Potosí's 2019 recognition procedure is functioning in practice, how long it takes, or what documents or conditions it requires; the source establishes that the procedure exists, not how it is administered.

No source here records enforcement of San Luis Potosí's hate-crime provisions in a trans-related case, so the practical value of that aggravating-clause coverage is unresolved.

Whether gender identity has since been added to the state's anti-discrimination statute is not sourced; the inventory states only the earlier position, in which sexual orientation and gender are covered and gender identity is not.

The inventory contains no San Luis Potosí-specific figures on violence against trans people, no data on refusal rates for name or gender change in the state, and no reporting on police or health-care treatment of trans visitors there. National violence figures (593 transfeminicidios 2008 to September 2021; 52 from October 2022 to September 2023) are not broken down by state.
